transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Hassan, thank you for coming in today. Your brother, thank you for joining us. I asked you both here because I have some very important and difficult information to share regarding your recent biopsy results.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Here we go. What is it this time?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am incredibly sorry to tell you that a serious error occurred in the pathology laboratory. Your biopsy specimen was mislabelled. As a result, the cancer diagnosis you received last week actually belongs to another patient. You do not have cancer.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You're joking.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am not. I am profoundly sorry for this mistake. It is entirely our responsibility as a medical team that this happened.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I spent three days thinking my life was over. Three days. My brother and I didn't even sleep.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know those words can't undo those three days, but I want to be clear that I am deeply sorry for the distress and the fear this has caused you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: This is just... it is just like the other time. Every time I come here, something goes wrong. I'm just a number to you people.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I realize that given your history with this clinic, hearing this today feels like another blow. It makes sense that you'd feel like the system is failing you.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: It is failing me. Now I'm sitting here and you're telling me I don't have cancer, but I can't even believe you're telling me that. Why should I believe you now?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is a completely fair question. The lab has since conducted a full audit of the mislabelled batch to ensure the error was isolated. To make sure I've explained this clearly, do you understand how the mix-up happened?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You said the labels were swapped. So some other person thinks they're fine while I'm panicking.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: My brother has been calling specialists. He's been on the phone for forty-eight hours trying to find an oncologist. Who is going to fix that?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know it's frustrating to have spent that energy on a mistake we made. I want to make sure we get the correct information in front of you now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Just tell me what happens next. Do I have to do the whole thing over?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes, we need to perform a repeat biopsy to get an accurate diagnosis for your specific case. I've already cleared a priority slot for you this Friday morning at 8:00 AM.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Friday. Great. More needles.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I know you're weary of more procedures. I will personally oversee the labelling and transport of the new sample to the lab myself to ensure this cannot happen again.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: You'll actually go down there?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I will. I'll carry the specimen from the procedure room directly to the pathology intake and verify the identity markers personally.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: And when will I actually know the truth?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: The pathology team has agreed to a 48-hour rush on this specific sample. I will call you personally on Monday afternoon by 4:00 PM with the results.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Monday. I'll believe it when I hear it.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand why you feel cynical about this. I am committed to seeing this through correctly. Is there anything else about the mix-up or the next steps that I can clarify for you right now?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know. I'm just exhausted.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I can imagine. Why don't we give you a few minutes to talk privately, and then I'll come back in to finalize the paperwork for Friday?

H.justification: Resident never interrupts, allows the patient to express frustration fully, and maintains a regulated pace throughout the encounter.

E.justification: Error (mislabelled biopsy) named in the second turn, lay language used, and comprehension checked twice ('do you understand how the mix-up happened?' and 'anything else... I can clarify?').

A.justification: Direct apologies are used ('incredibly sorry', 'profoundly sorry'), responsibility is explicitly claimed ('entirely our responsibility'), and accountability is maintained despite patient pushback.

R.justification: Specific emotions are named ('distress and the fear', 'cynical') and the resident engages with the patient's history of feeling like a number.

T.justification: Plan includes specific next steps (repeat biopsy), timelines (Friday 8:00 AM, Monday 4:00 PM), patient role (attending the biopsy), and a specific prevention strategy (resident personally transporting the sample).
